items.title: Voters deliver "AI earthquake," rebuking tech and billionaires
items.summary:
AI had its "official debut" as the biggest issue in American politics, former New York Assemblymember and RAISE Act author Alex Bores told Axios. "AI is reaching into every part of our society and economy and it's now crystal clear it's impacting every part of our politics, too." [...] Voters showed deep distrust of the AI race Tuesday, approving dozens of data center moratoriums and electing a raft of candidates who favor slowing a $10 trillion buildout, including in Texas — the epicenter of the boom.

Why it matters: In an election that hinged on an affordability crisis for many Americans, voters made it clear they view Silicon Valley's AI ambitions not as a technological miracle, but as a resource-draining threat to their wallets and communities.

On Tuesday, Election Day, I wrote that for the first time in this AI Tech Wave, AI data centers were on the ballot, in ‘Data Centers on the Ballot in 15 Governor Races’. And I promised we’d assess the impact of the results later this week. Well, the votes are mostly counted. And the verdict on the AI buildout was louder than almost anyone expected.

Axios summed it up the morning after, in ‘Voters deliver “AI earthquake,” rebuking tech and billionaires’: [...] Voters approved dozens of data center moratoriums, and elected a raft of candidates who favor slowing the $10 trillion AI buildout. Including in Texas, the epicenter of the boom. In an election that turned on affordability, voters signaled they see Silicon Valley’s AI ambitions less as a miracle, and more as a drain on their wallets and their communities. The ‘AI earthquake’ label came from Brad Carson of Americans for Responsible Innovation, and it stuck.

items.title: Voters deliver "AI earthquake," rebuking tech and billionaires
items.summary:
Voters showed deep distrust of the AI race Tuesday, approving dozens of data center moratoriums and electing a raft of candidates who favor slowing a $10 trillion buildout, including in Texas — the epicenter of the boom.

Why it matters: In an election that hinged on an affordability crisis for many Americans, voters made it clear they view Silicon Valley's AI ambitions not as a technological miracle, but as a resource-draining threat to their wallets and communities. [...] The results were a warning shot to some of the nation's wealthiest and most powerful executives, many of whom are already working on ways to build a more palatable version of the revolution they are dead-set on winning.

"What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake,"Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, told Axios. "Voters just sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers." [...] Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), a 2028 contender who won reelection by a wide margin, called out "the titans of Silicon Valley" in a victory speech, saying they "dig bunkers for themselves" even as they warn "that the artificial intelligence they're creating risks human extinction."

Nvidia chips can be legally sold to non-Chinese customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. And Chinese companies can legally access the most [...] Jensen Huang has pushed the Trump administration to loosen U.S. export controls to China. He has said that the controls have backfired and caused Chinese companies to invest more heavily in their own AI development and blocked Nvidia from accessing the second-largest computer market in the world. The Nvidia executive has also argued that capping chip sales runs counter to the goal of having the rest of the world build on U.S. technology.

items.summary:
Share this article

WorldParticle, built by researchers at MIT and UBC, uses one AI architecture to simulate materials ranging from sand to proteins. The system predicts particle motion step by step and could aid soft robotics, medicines and scientific discovery.

Researchers at MIT and the University of British Columbia published an open-access paper Nov. 9, 2026, describing WorldParticle, an AI system that simulates many materials with one architecture, from sliding sand to folding proteins. [...] WorldParticle represents every material it simulates, from a dune of sand to a protein molecule, as tiny particles and predicts where those particles will move one step at a time. Because it learns the underlying dynamics rather than being programmed with an equation, the model can adapt to materials, forces and environments it never encountered during training. In the long term, the researchers hope this work helps scientists discover new materials and explore physical processes they could not [...] The team demonstrated WorldParticle by modeling six different physical phenomena, including deformable objects and granular materials, with higher accuracy than numerical simulation methods. For instance, WorldParticle captured how a granular object would collapse into a pile while some baseline methods left sand particles floating in the air. The method also modeled how protein structures change over time about 100 times faster than numerical simulators, Guo said.

## Real-world applicability
